title: On War
author: Clausewitz, Carl von (Edited and Translated by Michael Howard and Peter Paret)
notes:
a. (p 310) "Take a division of 10,000 or 12,000 men, augmented by cavalry, which has been sent a day's march of fifteen to twenty miles [24 to 32 km] ahead. In ordinary, not particularly difficult country, it will be able to delay the enemy for about half as long again (including the time of his own retreat) as would otherwise be required to cover the distance. ... So a distance of twenty miles [32.2 km], which would ordinarily amount to a march of about ten hours, can be expected to take the enemy fifteen hours from the time he appears in strength before one's advanced division until he is in position to attack our main force."

b. (p 316) "Experience also teaches that the head of a column of four divisions with a cavalry reserve can generally do fifteen miles [24.14 km] in eight hours, even on inferior roads. At the rate of an hour per division, and the same for the cavalry and artillery reserves, the march will take thirteen hours to complete. This is not too long a time, and yet enough for a total of 40,000 men to march along one road."

c. (p 319) "Modern armies have long been accustomed to consider a fifteen-mile [24.14 km] march as a day's work. In extensive operations, it must be reduced to an average of ten miles [16.09 km] in order to allow for the requisite days of rest on which necessary repairs and maintenance can be carried out.

"A division of 8,000 men takes eight to ten hours for such a march in level country and on ordinary roads. In mountainous country, it will take ten to twelve [hours]. If a column consists of a number of divisions, a few hours longer will be required, even discounting the delayed starting time of the later divisions.

"It is clear that the day is pretty well filled by such a march. and that one cannot compare the strain on a soldier loaded with his pack for ten or twelve hours with an ordinary fifteen-mile [24.14 km] walk which would not take an individual more than five hours on a decent road.

"Forced marches, if undertaken one at a time. may cover twenty-five miles [40.23 km], or thirty [48.28 km] at the most; if they continue, only twenty [32.2 km].

"A march of twenty-five miles [40.23 km] will call for a rest stop of several hours, and a division of 8,000 men will not manage it in less than sixteen hours even on good roads. If the distance to be covered is thirty miles [48.28 km] and several divisions are involved, one has to allow a minimum of twenty hours."

d. (p 320) "[The] Prussian army, on its retreat in 1806, [had it done some things differently] need not have made immense exertions to cover some 250 miles [402.34 km] in no less than fourteen days [17.86 mi/day or 28.74 km/day]."

e. (p 320) "So the Seven Year's War produced marches that have still not been surpassed: Lascy's, for instance, in 1760, in support of the Russian diversion toward Berlin. He covered the 220 miles [354.06 km] from Schweidnitz through Lusatia to Berlin in ten days--a rate of 22 miles a day, which would be astounding even nowadays for a corps of 15,000 men [22 mi/day = 35.41 km/day]."

f. (p 320) "Hence the fact that Bonaparte, when pursuing the Prussians and trying to cut off their retreat in 1806, and Blücher, intending to do the same to the French in 1813, both required ten days to cover only 150 miles [241.40 km] or so. That was a rate which Frederick the Great achieved, baggage and all, when marching from Saxony to Silesia and back."

g. (p 321) "In general, the reduction in baggage will result in a saving of effort rather than an acceleration of movement."

h. (p 322) "A single moderate march will not blunt the instrument [i.e., the fighting forces]; but a series of moderate marches will begin to tell, while a series of strenuous marches will naturally do much greater harm."

i. (p 323) "A march of 500 miles [804.67] or more will always cause an army to arrive at its destination in a highly weakened condition, especially where horses and wagons are concerned. ... Bonaparte's advance was indeed unrelenting, from the crossing of the Niemen up to Moscow; but one must bear in mind that it took 82 days to cover only about 600 miles [965.61 km], and that the army stopped altogether--once for some 14 days at Vilna and the other time for some 11 days at Vitebsk--which must have given many stragglers time to catch up."

j. (p 324) "Great wear and tear on one's own forces, therefore, must be expected if one intends to wage a mobile war. All other plans must be adjusted to that fact; and above all, replacements must be provided for."

k. (p 545) "Naturally we assume that the defender will act as sensibly and correctly as the attacker. We say this in order to exclude certain vague notions about sudden assaults and surprise attacks, which are commonly thought of as bountiful sources of victory. They will only be that under exceptional circumstances."

Several of these reports mention infantry or cavalry marches made by forces in the general area of the battle. It appears that in those days engineer officers had the job of recording the progress of forces on the march in a log or diary, and for always knowing where they were on the prairie or in the badlands. It seems they were also supposed to note in their log information on weather; river widths and depths; geological observations; and any other information useful in evaluating the locale's potential for economic development. These engineer reports appear to be the best information on distances and dates.

id: DECISIVE BATTLES OF THE SOVIET ARMY
title: World War II: Decisive Battles of the Soviet Army
author: Larionov, V., N. Yeronin, B. Solovyev, V. Timokhovich
notes:
a. (p 312) Re: Operation Bagration of Mid-1944, in pursuit of a retreating enemy by tank, motorised, or cavalry corps and armies, rates of advance averaged 25 to 40 km/day, and on some days it ranged from 50 to 70 km/day. The tank armies and corps usually bypassed centers of resistance and did not get bogged down in protracted engagement for settlements.

b. (p 357) Re: Jassy-Kishinev Operation of August 1944, in the second stage of the operation the rate of advance by mobile (tank and motorised) units averaged more than 40 km/day. So high a rate of advance was the result of the complete routing of the enemy in the first stage of the operation.

c. (pp 383-384) Re: Vistula-Oder Operation of January 1945, the first day's advance was 15 to 20 km on a 35-km sector. After 2 days, the advance increased to 25 to 40 km and the breakthrough widened to 60 km. On the fourth day, the fresh 1st Tank Army was committed and its forward brigades "made a dash of 40 to 50 km."

d. (p 388) Re: Vistula-Oder Operation, in pursuit of the enemy the tank armies, tank and mechanised corps broke away from the field armies up to distances of 50 to 80 km. "In their wake the rifle units, supported from the air by the Front aviation, moved ahead at the top possible speed--up to 30 km/day."

e. (p 399) Re: Vistula-Oder Operation, daily average speed of 25 km, and for tank units this speed was 45 to 70 km/day.

f. (p 400) Re: Vistula-Oder Operation, the First Ukranian Front's rate of advance varied between 11 and 15 km/day. The First Byelorussian Front's rate of advance varied between 13 and 17 km/day. After the Vistula defense line had been surmounted, the rate of advance of the Field Armies increased to 25-35 km/day.

g. (p 418) Re: Berlin Operation of April-May 1945, the *planned* average rates of advance of the 2d Army (Polish) were 14 km/day for field armies and 30 km/day for tank armies. The *planned* rate of advance by the 2d Shock Army was 8 to 11 km/day.

h. (p 510) Re: Manchurian Campaign of August 1945, the rate of advance varied between 17 km/day for the 25th Army to "more than 90 km/day" for the 6th Guards Tank Army.

title: I Rode With Stonewall
author: Douglas, Henry Kyd
date: 1940 (from the 1899 manuscript as edited by John Kyd Beckenbaugh)
organization: The University of North Carolina Press, Chapel Hill, North Carolina
notes:
a. (p 9) "We marched as rapidly as the country would permit, seventeen miles [from Winchester] to Paris and then early the next morning to Piedmont, six miles, and there took the [railroad] cars."

b. (p 36) " ... he [General Jackson] started off again down [i.e., northwards through] the [Shenandoah] Valley--making a twenty-five mile (40 km) march [from Mount Jackson] the first day. The next day, the 23rd, he [Jackson] was off early and did not stop until he ran up against the enemy near Kernstown and prepared for battle."

c. (p 45) "In less than twenty hours I had ridden about one hundred and five miles (169 km), and since I left General Jackson I had passed around the Massanutton [mountain], over the Blue Ridge, and through rain and mud and impenetrable night had been under the strain of a cavalry charge [figuratively] for more than eighty miles.

"When I revived [from a fainting spell] and had something to eat, ... I remained in bed for twenty-four hours."

d. (p 47) "It was only about sixteen miles (25.75 km) [along the east side of the Shenandoah River from Conrad's Store to Port republic], but it took him [Jackson and his forces] two days and a half to do it. [6.4 mi/day or 10.30 km/day] ... over soft and bottomless roads into which horses and wagons and artillery sank, at times almost out of sight, dragged along by main force of horses and men, the General himself on foot, lifting and pushing among the struggling mass, wet, covered with mud from cap to boots, encouraging soldiers and teamster by word and example,."

e. (p 69) "From Loudoun Heights [near Harper's Ferry] and Charlestown to a point between Kernstown and Newtown--a distance of thirty-five miles [56.3 km]--they made a continuous march and going into camp about midnight rested until morning. It was one of those forced marches which all of General Jackson's army were sometimes called upon to endure, and which won for them the appropriate name of 'Foot Cavalry.'"

f. (p 92) "In thirty days his [Jackson's] army had marched nearly four hundred miles [13.33 mi/day, 644 km, 21.46 km/day], skirmishing almost daily, fought five battles, defeated four armies, two of which were completely routed, captured about twenty pieces of artillery, some four thousand prisoners, and immense quantities of stores of all kinds, and had done all this with a loss of less than one thousand killed, wounded and missing."

g. (p 112-113) "Experience is not lost upon the rank and file, and they generally got a correct idea of the situation: they even anticipated movements [out of contact with the enemy] that were afterwards ordered by their General. On the battlefield too, they took in the perils of a situation, and that is doubtless the reason why veteran troops gave away and became panic-stricken at times, while fresh volunteers who did not see the danger remained on the field and kept fighting. Old troops often know when they are whipped; new ones often do not and are ignorant of the dangers which lurk in flank and rear. More than once have battles, nearly lost by veterans, been restored by the intrepid obstinacy of new soldiers."

h. (p 169) "Longstreet's troops were sent to Jackson, too, and there were no unfought soldiers, no spectators, no reserves in the Army of Northern Virginia that memorable day [at Antietam]."

i. (p 173) "Just then A. P. Hill in his red and picturesque battle shirt, with 2,500 of his men, who had marched seventeen miles [27.36 km] that day and waded the Potomac River, appeared upon the scene [at Antietam]. ... Jones rallied on Hill and [together] they drove Burnside back to the Antietam and the protection of his heavy guns so rapidly that Hill's other brigades could not catch up and get a share in the fighting."

j. (p 241) "Starting at four o'clock on the 5th [of June] our division moved off and marched for fifteen miles [24.14 km], through Spotsylvania. On the next day we were detained for a while by rumors that the enemy were making demonstrations at Fredericksburg [VA], but we got off later and marched ten miles [16.09 km]. The next day, being Sunday, we marched seventeen miles [27.36 km] and crossed the Rapidan.

"On the 9th we were kept under arms awaiting the result of a severe cavalry fight [Brandy Station] which lasted nearly all that day. ... The next day we only managed about ten miles [16.09 km]; the day following we made eighteen [28.97 km], encamping at Gaines Cross Roads. Starting at 4:30 A.M. on the 12th, we marched eighteen miles and encamped near Cedarville. On the next morning Rodes's division moved toward Berryville, and Johnson and Early to Winchester. We found Winchester well fortified. The 14th was spent demonstrating against the town. ... After dark our division drew off, and after marching about three miles [4.83 km] on the Berryville pike we made a detour by way of Jordan Springs toward the Winchester and Martinsburg pike. We came to the pike about four miles [6.44 km] from Winchester a little before daylight, and there ran into General Milroy's army, retreating from Winchester."

k. (p 289-290) "[General] Early left after midnight for Charlottesville and made a forced march of eighty miles [128.75 km] to that place in four days [20 mi/day, 32.2 km/day]. His [Early's] corps had been greatly reduced in the campaign and numbered about 8,000 effective muskets."

title: Operations
author: Anonymous
notes: (p 94) [Using the example of Grant's Vicksburg Campaign] "Setting a pace of operations so rapid that his enemies could not follow his activities, Grant defeated the forces of Generals Johnson and Pemberton in five successive engagements. He covered 200 miles in 19 days [10.5 mi/day, or 322 km in 19 days, 16.9 km/day], capturing Jackson and driving the defenders of Vicksburg into their trenches. Grant's 4,000 casualties were only half as great as his enemy's. ... The same speed, surprise, maneuver, and decisive action will be required in the campaigns of the future."

title: Quiet End to a Long Walk for Peace
author: Saperstein, Sandra
notes:

title: Personal Communication to Dr. Robert L. Helmbold
author: From Mrs. Harriet Fast Scott
notes:
(On the Soviet Manchurian Action Late in WW II)

a. Maps don't give the correct borders. The distances and times are about right, although its important to understand that the larger distances apply only to a few "spearhead" elements that were sustained by a very special effort.

b. The Soviets were just going across Outer Mongolia, and here there was no opposition, "by and large." To all intents and purposes, the war had ended, and Soviet claims of amount of resistance are exaggerated.

c. The Soviets ran out of gas, but pooled fuel to send an advance guard of a few vehicles ahead just to claim the territory for postwar negotiations. Soviets even flew in gas by air to sustain the last drive.

title: Commentary on Infantry Operations and Weapons Usage in Korea, Winter of 1950-51
author: S. L. A. Marshall
notes:
(pp 33-36, passim) "Under the best of conditions, in making the approach from the bivouac area to the LD [Line of Departure for an attack], the company will usually have to march [on foot, in addition to whatever truck distance is used] somewhat between one-half and one-and-a-half miles, carrying its own equipment. These things considered, for the Korean terrain, the potential of the infantry company--how far it can move in the attack carrying a fighting load and still remain tactically sound for night defense--can be reckoned approximately as follows:

| Terrain | Distances | Load |
|---|---|---|
| Over ridges exceeding 400 meters height | 1,800-2,200 yards actual distance | Basic fighting |
| Over ridges averaging 200 meters or slightly less | 3,000-3,500 yards actual distance | Basic fighting |
| Over ridges averaging 100 meters or less | 5,000-7,000 yards actual distance | Basic fighting |
| Road march, flat country | 8-9 miles actual distance | Basic load, rations and bedroll |

"This scale is premised on the unit not being engaged by heavy or occasional killing fire during the approach march; it applies to movement made under the stresses of the weight carried and the general apprehension of engagement. Sharp fire or sudden losses will radically reduce the potential. These are maximum distances and requirements within the range of slightly cold to moderate temperatures averaging between 20* and 60*. In the summer season and in extreme cold, the figures should be halved for marches at the higher elevations. There will be some reduction during the rainy season when roads and trails are muddy; ice conditions will also lower the figure. Furthermore the altitude of the hill or ridge is a somewhat arbitrary yardstick, since in some cases there would be less stress in climbing a 500-meter hill with gradually ascending slopes than a 150-meter height via a series of rocky sub-ridges and cross-cutting ravines. It is believed, however, that the scale is sufficiently accurate to provide a base for continuing study of this subject. ...

"The city-bred ROK [Republic of Korea] soldier, integrated in the American unit, appeared to react physically to these stresses no better than the average man from this country [the US]. He wore out as quickly and, when fatigued, was even less ready to take an active part in the firing. On the other hand, the country-bred ROK, who was accustomed to moving long distances afoot, had markedly more endurance, and would also tend to respond strongly in emergency situations."

title: Washing of the Spears
author: Morris, Donald R.
notes:
a. (p 309) "Ulundi lay less than 75 miles from the three invasion points, and the country, while rolling and seamed with small rivers and dongas, was generally open. A mounted man could reach Ulundi from the Tugela in a long day's hard riding, a Zulu impi or a Boer commando in two or three day's travel. Even unopposed, however, a British infantry battalion would take the better part of a fortnight to get in and out, and Chelmsford, of course, expected no such rapid progress."

b. (p 312) "A full span of oxen ran from fourteen to eighteen beasts. Less than ten were rarely yoked, for while they might still move the wagon with a ton of goods aboard, they would be stopped by the slightest rise. On steep hills and at drifts where the wheels sank into mud or sand, double spans were needed, and up to forty oxen might be needed to breast the mountain passes. ... An ox required eight hours a day to graze, and a further eight hours to rest while the results of his grazing passed through his multiple stomachs and was regurgitated as cud for a second leisurely mastication. This left eight hours a day for work, during which a full, fresh span might move more than a ton of goods at a steady three miles an hour along a level road. If the team was kept spanned for the full eight hours, it would need several days to recover from the experience, and the teams were usually outspanned for a couple of hours at midday. Under ideal conditions, this meant that a wagon might move as much as eighteen miles a day, but since there were hardly eighteen miles of surfaced road in all of southern Africa, few wagons ever covered more than ten miles a day. A stony track, a sandy drift, or a rainstorm might reduce progress to three or four miles a day, or even stop it entirely."

c. (pp 360-362) "As Wood's spies had predicted, it [the main Zulu impi, numbering about 20,000, dispatched to the battle of Isandhlwana] had departed the vicinity of Ulundi on the seventeenth [17 January 1879]. It had mustered at the great military kraal of Nodwengu, hard by the royal kraal [at Ulundi], and there Cetshwayo had given it its final instructions. ... The army was to march slowly, so as not to tire itself, and it was to attack only in daylight. ... The impi left Nodwengu late on the seventeenth and bivouaced on the banks of White Umfolozi that night. ... The impi covered a leisurely nine miles on the eighteenth, and a similar distance on the nineteenth, stopping at military kraals both nights. On the twentieth it split into two columns which made long parallel marches, and it spent the night in a hollow just to the north of Isipezi Hill. ... they moved the main impi up to the Nqutu plateau on the forenoon of the twenty-first, finding the deep ravine running north and south four miles from the head of the spur and bedding the regiments down in the course of the afternoon." They were discovered there by the British a bit later, largely by accident.

d. Based on maps in the source, I estimate that the impi moved 25 miles on the 25th and 10 miles on the 21st. Hence the following estimated itinerary.

| Day | Miles | Km |
|---|---|---|
| 17th | 4 | 6.4 |
| 18th | 9 | 14.5 |
| 19th | 9 | 14.5 |
| 20th | 25 | 40.2 |
| 21st | 10 | 16.1 |
| Total 5 | 57 | 92 |

Thus, I estimate an average of 11.4 mi/day or 18.4 km/day.

title: The Basic Principles of Operational Art and Tactics (A Soviet View)
author: Savkin, Vasilii Y. (Translated and published under the auspices of the US Air Force)
organization: Superintendent of Documents, US Government Printing Office, Washington, DC
notes:
a. (pp 57-59, passim) "The action of statistical laws in armed conflict arises as a result of a mass employment of personnel, combat equipment, and weaponry under approximately identical conditions, as well as with the manifold repetition of events, when certain attributes common to all of them are discovered."

"For example, indicators of the tempo of offensive operations conducted by the Soviet Army in the second half of the Great Patriotic War could differ to a considerable extent in each concrete case and for a particular combined arms or tank army, but still they varied about specific average values characteristic of combat actions of that period and for the conditions which were in existence by that time. Thus in operations of the second half of the war our combined-arms armies advanced with an average daily rate of 20-30 km and tank armies advanced with a rate of 25-50 km, and sometimes 80-100 km per day."

"The width of zones of advance of armies in the second half of the war varied from 7 to 145 km, but comprised 30-50 km on the average for a majority of the armies."

"The density of fire of small arms (bullets per minute per meter of defensive front) set up in front of the forward edge of defense varied from two to 12, but the average was 5-6."

"Statistical laws express the nature of unregulated, chaotic processes. For example, thermal, electromagnetic, and quantum movements are unregulated."

b. (p 108) "For example, in the Battle of the Marne in September 1914 (at that time there were no tanks), the average daily rate of advance of the attackers reached 6 km, but on individual days increased to 20-22 km a day. In the March offensive of the Germans in 1918--they had no tanks--the average rate of advance was 4-4.5 km a day. However, in the Amiens operation (August 1918), in spite of the participation of over 600 tanks, the allies achieved a rate of advance of only 3-3.5 km a day."

c. (pp 118-119) "During the November offensive of the fascist German troops, which was conducted in considerably more favorable conditions of the weather (the winter had not yet set in, there was not considerable snow cover, while the slight freeze bound the autumn mud), such as on the Dmitrov and Solnechnogorsk axes, they advanced an average of no more than 4-5 km a day. However, our troops, who attacked under incomparably more difficult conditions of a severe winter, achieved double the average rate of advance--10-12 km a day. It is necessary to take into account here that Hitlerite shock groupings consisted of tank and motorized soyedineniya, while the Soviet troops basically had rifle chasti."

d. (pp 136-137) "The rates of advance and troop losses also were inversely proportional."

"An analysis of the size of losses and expenditure of supplies of tank armies in nine operations of the Great Patriotic War attests that in an attack with a tempo of 20-50 km per day the overall losses in personnel were a little over three times less, and in tanks were almost 1 1/2 times less than with a tempo of advance of 4-10 km per day."

"Rates of advance have an even greater effect on the specific consumption of supplies per 100 km of troop advance. As can be seen in Table 1 [not reproduced here], with high rates of advance of tank armies the specific consumption of ammunition was decreased by six times, and that of diesel fuel by three times."

"The experience of combat operations of combined-arms armies also attests to a reduction in losses with an increase in rates of advance."

"Let us turn to the experience of two operations of Thirty-Ninth Army in 1944. In an operation conducted in February, Thirty-Ninth Army was attacking with a tempo of 0.5 km per day, and in the Vitebsk Operation--9 km a day. At the higher rates of advance in the Vitebsk Operation, losses in personnel of Thirty-Ninth Army were six times less than in the operation conducted in February, and losses of tanks were 20 times less."

"Rates of advance are not the only factor determining troop losses. The latter also depend on many causes and conditions, but rates of advance play a most important role. ... "

"It must be added that with high rates of advance there is a considerable increase in losses by the defending enemy. ... "

e. (p 114) "For example, during the attack by Fifth Army during the period from 15 through 27 October 1944, it suffered considerably greater losses in comparison with other combined-arms armies and other operations by this same army. In 12 days, the army advanced 30 km, with an average daily advance of 2.5 km. With each day of the operation the rate of advance dropped. On 17 October troops of this army advanced 4-10 km, on the 18th 3-6 km, on the 19th, 2.5 km, on the 20th and 21st 2 km each day, on the 23rd, 24th, 25th, and 26th one km daily, and on the 27th 0.5 km."

f. (p 174) "L. Varvarzhovskiy writes about World War II: 'During the war approximately 40 percent of the time was taken up with moving troops, about 30-35 percent for combat operations, and around 25-30 percent for rest, reinforcing, reforming, etc.' It should be noted that these figures are for rifle and infantry soyedineniya. The proportion of movements in the combat activity of our tank and mechanized corps was considerably higher."

title: The Landscape Turned Red: The Battle of Antietam
author: Sears, Stephen W.
organization: Ticknor and Fields, New Haven and New York
notes:
a. (p 56) "The Jackson legend grew during the Valley Campaign, where he marched his army twenty-five miles [40.23 km] and more a day and in mysterious ways, bewildering his foes and attracting an avid following among Southern newspaper readers."

b. (p 62) "[At the battle of Second Manassas] ... Old Jack [Stonewall Jackson] exhorted his 'foot cavalry' and they responded by covering fifty-four miles [86.90 km] in two days."

c. (p 124) "Even his [Stonewall's] foot cavalry could not cover sixty miles [96.56 km] in two days [in action around Harper's Ferry and Martinsburg]."

d. (p 195-197) [Re: A. P. Hill's march from Harper's Ferry to Sharpsburg] "Fifteen minutes later [i.e., at 0730 in the morning], at Harpers' Ferry, A. P. Hill's Light Division set off for Sharpsburg, seventeen miles [27.36 km] away. Lee's courier had reached Hill at 0630, and he had his men on the road within the hour. The pace was fast, and the march regulation of a ten-minute rest every hour that Jackson prescribed for his foot cavalry was ignored. Hill rode back and forth along the column exhorting his men."

e. (p 285-289) [Re: A. P Hill's march from Harper's Ferry] "His Light Division's remarkable march from Harper's Ferry--seventeen miles [27.36 km] in less than eight hours--rivaled the best marks of Jackson's famous foot cavalry. That along the way Hill actually prodded laggards with the point of his sword is possibly apocryphal--probably the troop's two days of rest following the capture of Harper's Ferry had more to do with their achievement ... To be sure, uncounted hundreds were left by the roadside exhausted, and Hill then rushed his brigades into action piecemeal, ... It was at about 1530 hours that they [the Union's Ninth Corps under Burnside] first sighted enemy [i.e., Hill's Confederate] troops off to the south, moving toward the Ninth Corp's open flank ... it was close to 1630 hours, and the Ninth Corps was on the defensive and falling back."

f. (p 301-302) "The Federal troops who deserve the praise for commendable rapidity were the Pennsylvanians of Brigadier Andrew A. Humphrey's Fifth Corps division. This was a brand-new outfit, ... [This division] reached Frederick on September 16. The call to join the main army reached him shortly after two o'clock on the afternoon of the battle [17 September], and in the fashion of A. P. Hill he had his men on the road within the hour, ... Before ten o'clock that morning [18 September], after a hard night march of twenty-three miles [37.01 km], his division was in place in the [Union] army's reserve. More than that, he had lost only 600 of this 6,600 men to straggling."

title: The Offensive (A Soviet View)
author: Sidorenko, A. A. (Translated and published under the auspices of the US Air Force)
organization: Superintendent of Documents, US Government Printing Office, Washington, DC
notes:
a. (p 2) "Also very important is the circumstance that, as a rule, successfully attacking troops suffer fewer[1] losses than the defenders. Many examples may be presented in confirmation of this."

b. (p 11) "Along with this [increase of battle size and scale with time], the rates of the offensive increased continuously. In the First World War the average rates of attack did not exceed 4-6 km per day. The highest rate attained during the entire war was 18 km (the 7th German Army in the operation on the En River on 27 May 1918). [Ref. P. Varolomeyev, Udarnaya armiya (Shock Army), Moscow State Publishing House, 1933, p. 109] During the period of the Great Patriotic War, especially in the operations of 1944-45, the average rates of attack of the rifle troops reached 15-25 km per day and of the tank and mechanized troops--30-40 km per day (on individual days, 70-80 km). In the war with Japan in August 1945, the troops of the Transbaikal Front advanced 500-800 km in 10 days with an average rate of 50-80 km per day. The rate of attack of the 6th Guards Tank Army on individual days reached 100 km or more. [Ref. P. Rotmistrov, The Influence of Tanks on the Rates of Offensive Operations, Voyenno-istoricheskiy zhurnal (Journal of Military History), 1961, No. 1, p 14.]"

c. (p 12) "The increase in the rates of attack had an influence on reducing the duration of operations despite the increase in their depth. If, in 1944, large offensive operations of front groups lasted 40-80 days, in 1943 operations of the same depth continued for 20-30 days. The duration of front and army operations which, by the end of the war reached respectively 15-20 and 5-10 days, was reduced."

d. (p 81) "But in contrast to the [increase in] depth of the combat mission, as shown by the experience of the Great Patriotic War, the width of zone of advance had a clear tendency to decrease both on an operational and on a tactical scale. For example, while the width of zone of advance in the winter campaign of 1941/42 was 300-400 km on an average, in operations of 1944-45 it had decreased to 200-250 km. The width of the zone of advance of an army correspondingly decreased from 40-60 km to 20-40 km, and that of a rifle division from 4-6 km to 2 km. This was caused by the necessity to ensure creation of a decisive superiority in men and materiel over the enemy when breaking through his defense."

e. (p 156) "In the third period of the [Great Patriotic] war, when rates of attack rose and comprised up to 30-40 km on an average for tank and mechanized troops, and up to 15-25 km a day for rifle troops, the breakthrough of intermediate defensive positions was usually accomplished from the march."

[1] The original reads "more fuel," which evidently is a misprint. For, in addition to making no sense in context, it is flatly contradicted by the examples which immediately follow this passage.

title: Red Armour
author: Simpkin, Richard E.
notes:
a. (p 120) [With regard to operational "switches," not further clarified in the text] "But to my surprise none of the obvious factors--such as day or night, good roads or bad, dry weather or wet, even (as remarked earlier) the number of routes allocated--seemed to make any difference detectable as a pattern by eye, let alone [statistically] significant."

b. (p 122) Re: All-arms forces. "Formations were concentrated in a rear concentration area over 100 and up to 300 km behind the line of contact. They spent an average of 24 hours there and moved at an achieved speed of 10 km/hr to the forward concentration area 25 to 30 km behind the line of contact, where they spent up to 4 or 5 days. From there they moved to the assembly area (also the preparation area for an obstacle crossing) some 5 km behind the start line at an achieved speed of 5 km/hr. In the assembly area they spent either 20 to 30 hours or 10 to 12 hours, these alternatives presumably depending on the time of arrival in relation to a first light attack. Finally they moved to the start line at an achieved speed as low as 2.5 km/hr."

c. (p 122) "The second echelon tank forces in the sample moved on average 105 km from rear to forward concentration areas, taking some 12 hours at a real average speed of 10 km/hr. A 70 km move from there to the assembly area took 15 hours (5 km/hr); and a 25 km march forward to the pass-through or launch line took a further 12 hours (2.5 km/hr)."

d. (p 132) "The 100 km/day target with which NATO has loved to titillate its paranoia for three decades or so was laid down in the historic STAVKA directive, and the subsequent NKO Order No. 325 of 10 January 1942, covering the formation of tank and mechanised corps and their employment in the exploitation of penetrations along deep thrust lines. ... [Yet in WW II] the average for tank armies after breakthrough was barely half the target figure. More significant still, the highest individual figure I found, taken from an operation near the end of the war that was pretty well straight 'motoring,' is only 85 percent of target. ... The Israeli bogey rate for the Mitla stakes is about 130 km/day, and they established this with Centurion tanks, still with the British engine and having a maximum speed of only 37 km/hr."

title: "The Story of Civilization: Part I-Our Oriental Heritage"
author: Durant, Will
notes: (p 154) "For twenty-two years the Queen [Hatshepsut] ruled in wisdom and peace; Thutmose III followed with a reign of many wars. Syria took advantage of Hatshepsut's death to revolt; it did not seem likely to the Syrians that Thutmose, a lad of twenty-two, would be able to maintain the empire created by his father [Thutmose III was the son of Thutmose I by a concubine]. But Thutmose set off in the very year of his accession, marched his army through Kantara and Gaza at twenty miles a day, and confronted the rebel forces at Har-Megiddo (i.e., Mt. Megiddo), a little town so strategically placed between the rival Lebanon ranges on the road from Egypt to the Euphrates that it has been the Armageddon of countless wars from that day to General A. Allenby's. In the same pass where in 1918 the British defeated the Turks, Thutmose III, 3397 years before, defeated the Syrians and their allies. Then Thutmose marched victorious through western Asia, subduing, taxing and levying tribute, and returned to Thebes in triumph six months after his departure."
comments:
a. In a footnote to this passage, Durant remarks that "Allenby took twice as long to accomplish a similar result; Napoleon, attempting it at Acre, failed."

b. It is interesting to note the reference to an advance rate of 20 mi/day (32.2 km/day) at this early date in history.

title: The First Salute
author: Tuchman, Barbara W.
notes:
a. (pp 208-209) [Re: Cornwallis, with at least 1,500 men in pursuit of Morgan through North Carolina in 1781, directly following the battle of Cowpens] "Recent heavy rains had made high water in the rivers and turned the roads into troughs of mud that sucked at the marcher's boots and slowed progress. ... Cornwallis' large Army, plowing heavily through the mud churned by Morgan's passage, was slowed and delayed by every river, but kept on coming. In steady rain mixed with snow, they were making no more than six miles [9.66 km] a day."

b. (pp 248-279) [Re: Washington's move from the vicinity of New York to Yorktown where he planned to confront Cornwallis. The crossing of the Hudson River took place 20 August 1781.] "Because of the limited and primitive roads of the period, and to ease the pressure of foraging on the countryside and to add to Clinton's [the British theater commander, headquartered in New York] uncertainty about the objective, the Allied Army [Continental and French], in two groups, took separate routes along two parallel lines. Foot soldiers covered fifteen miles [24.14 km, from the west bank of the Hudson] the first day, a distance that over the next two weeks remained about the daily average. ... They come next to Princeton ... After a 'very good breakfast' they push on to Trenton, having covered 45 miles [72.42 km] that day. ... Crossing the Delaware on September 1, the marchers arrived in Philadelphia the next day, having covered so far 133 miles [214.04 km]. ... From Philadelphia, the Army moved on toward Chester, in Pennsylvania, on the way to its destination at Head of the Elk, at the top of the northernmost inlet of Chesapeake Bay [where it was to be picked up by the French fleet and ferried to southern Virginia] ... When the Allied army marching down from Philadelphia arrived at Head of the Elk in Maryland on September 6, they found only empty wharves ... In bitter conference, the generals agreed to embark on the few boats at hand about 3,000 troops, 2,100 French and 800 Americans, and send the rest of the army on foot down the road to Baltimore 55 miles [88.51 km] away. ... Covering 20 miles [32.2 km] a day on this stretch, the men reached Baltimore on September 12. Here at last they found water transport."

title: Supplying War
author: Van Creveld, Martin
notes:
a. (p 112) "In theory, there was no reason why marching columns should not be able to sustain a steady fifteen miles a day, a figure that had not changed since time immemorial. However, this was being made increasingly difficult by the huge proportions of the trains. Between 1870 and 1914, the number of wagons on the establishment of each corps had more than doubled, from 457 to 1168, and this was quite apart from the often still greater amount of transport required to refill the troops' mobile reserves as they became depleted. Though the horse-drawn transport operating in the army's rear was capable of considerably outmarching the men (twenty-five miles per day being reckoned as a steady average), it was forever shuttling forward and backward between front and base and was therefore certain to fall further behind with every day's march."

b. (p 234) "... it appears that the maximum sustained speed of eighteenth-century armies was three miles per hour--the pace of a marching man--and that they were occasionally able to cover as much as fifteen miles per day for two or three weeks on end. As against their ratio of 1:5. modern vehicles--even tracked ones--can easily cover fifteen miles an hour. but no army, not even the British 'Blade Force' chasing Rommel in North Africa or Malinowsky's armoured columns in pursuit of the Japanese in Manchuria, has managed to sustain a pace of seventy-five miles a day for more than a very few days at a time."

c. (p 235) "It was demonstrated in the Israeli-Egyptian campaign of 1967 that not even an army operating under ideal conditions, enjoying complete superiority in the air and taking a second rate opponent by surprise, stands much chance of covering more than forty miles per day. ... the speed and range of successive new means of transport have been largely, if not completely, offset by the enormous increase in friction and, above all, by the quantities of supplies required. Hence, even if an entirely new and unprecedentedly effective means of transport were to appear tomorrow, it is to be expected that only a small fraction of its maximum theoretical capacity will ever be utilized in practice, and that its effect on the speed of mobile operations will therefore be marginal."
